newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan port workers strike, rally against U.S. levy.
newsitem.headline: Japan port workers strike, rally against U.S. levy.

text.p: Japanese dock workers, angered by U.S pressure to deregulate port practices, held a one-day strike on Wednesday against what they see as Washington's strong-arm tactics.

The action paralysed cargo operations at ports around the country and turned up the heat in an already intractable trade dispute with the United States over the way freight is handled at Japanese ports.

Waving banners declaring "down with deregulation", around 300 dock workers held a demonstration at a Tokyo harbour to mark the start of the 24-hour stoppage, saying the changes sought by the United States would threaten their jobs.

Labour unions coordinating the strike said the industrial action -- a rare occurrence in Japan -- halted all loading and unloading of freight at about 50 ports, including the key transport hubs of Tokyo, Yokohama and Kobe.

The strike was called to protest against a U.S. decision to slap a $100,000 surcharge on each Japanese vessel entering a U.S. port from abroad in retaliation for what Washington has called unfair Japanese port practices. The striking workers are also calling for better work conditions.

"Reform would increase competition among port workers, leading to the deterioration of working conditions and eventually to turmoil at Japanese ports," Katsuyoshi Tamura, chairman of the Council of Dock Workers' Unions of Tokyo, told the demonstrators.

The Japan Shipowners' Association estimated that the nationwide strike by the National Council of Dock Workers' Unions and the Japan Confederation of Port and Transport Workers' Unions affected about 60 Japanese vessels and an estimated 70 foreign vessels.
The two labour unions comprise almost half of Japan's 100,000 dock workers.
The United States says the Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA) discriminates against foreign firms.
The JHTA, made up of port cargo-handling firms, serves as the mediator between unions and shipping companies.
It has shown no signs of relenting, to the dismay of Japanese shipping firms which say they are innocent victims in the dispute.

Japan's Transport Ministry plans to ease restrictions on business licences at Japanese ports within three to five years. Newcomers have been restricted in the past 10 years because of a surplus of stevedores, the ministry said.

Port workers have fiercely opposed the ministry's plans. "The Transport Ministry has no concrete policy on ports and does not understand the important role ports play in the country's trade," Tamura told the port workers' gathering. ($1=123 yen)
